catalog_quote: O accento tonico recae quasi sempre na penultima syllaba e por isso mesmo, com poucas excepções, os vocabulos são graves, o que se reconhece pelos exemplos já apresentados. Poucos são os agudos, como: dizêu «dente», dičiad̃iá «depois de amanhã». Porém os graves tornam-se agudos unindo-se a outros. Ex.: ŭape, ŭapé_kamo «bom, melhor»; ukŭete, ukŭeté_ŭoma «tem, tem medo», o que já se advertiu a pag. 6. Muito poucos são os esdruxulos ou proparoxytonos, como: sâb̃año «seis», tátuko «pai». Observações. — I. Os bângalas e os quiôcos já vão differindo dos lundas, fazendo predominar os accentos nas ultimas syllabas. [p. 7, Obs. II:] ... entendendo-se que a ausencia de accentuação graphica sobre a vogal tonica denota ser esta a da penultima syllaba do vocabulo, simples ou composto, primitivo ou derivado, quando a ultima syllaba não contenha dithongo cujo segundo elemento seja ĭ ou ŭ, porque neste caso é esta a syllaba predominante.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ruund (ruun1238) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Kasombo Tshibanda 2009 'Le Kanincin: Analyse grammaticale et interprétation prospective des unités prosodiques' (Lubumbashi doctoral dissertation on the Kanincin variety of Ruund, ≥253 pp., French), exists only as a Glottolog record: no online copy or library holding was found after searching Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, Google Books, archive.org, HathiTrust, LoC, SUDOC, UGent, UniCat, BASE, CORE and three web engines (Google Scholar blocked; Its relevance to word stress is unclear — the title's 'prosodic units' are, from the one second-hand citation available, tonal. That citation comes from the author's own co-authored open-access article Devos, Kasombo Tshibanda & van der Auwera 2010 (Africana Linguistica 16: 155-181, DOI 10.3406/aflin.2010.990), downloaded from Persée and read in full: it places Kanincin as 'a variety of Ruund (L53)' of Luilu territory, East Kasai, corrects the thesis's institution to Université de Lubumbashi, and says nothing about stress. Re-reading the materials already held by the project from the earlier reading: Carvalho 1890 (p. 11, image-verified) states the tonic accent falls almost always on the penultimate syllable with few oxytones, rare proparoxytones and a phrasal shift to final position; Nash 1994 gives no stress rule (Ruund is a L-marked two-tone language) but notes 'accent-like prominence' of abrupt-falling-pitch syllables (p. 269 fn. 44) and contrasts Swahili 'a language with penultimate stress' (p. 272); Ntotila & Vincke 1986 and Angenot & Vincke 1977 contain no accent statement. Best statement read: Carvalho 1890 p. 11 (penultimate), an impressionistic pre-tonal account and therefore weak evidence for a stress system. Acquisition priority for the Kasombo thesis: medium (only full prosodic study of a Ruund variety by a native speaker; would need a request to UNILU or to Maud Devos at RMCA Tervuren).

new_statements.quote: O accento tonico recae quasi sempre na penultima syllaba e por isso mesmo, com poucas excepções, os vocabulos são graves, o que se reconhece pelos exemplos já apresentados. Poucos são os agudos, como: dizêu «dente», dičiadiá «depois de amanhã». Porém os graves tornam-se agudos unindo-se a outros. Ex.: ŭape, ŭapé_kamo «bom, melhor»; ukŭete, ukŭeté_ŭoma «tem, tem medo», o que já se advertiu a pag. 6. Muito poucos são os esdruxulos ou proparoxytonos, como: sâbaño «seis», tátuko «pai». Observações. — I. Os bângalas e os quiôcos já vão differindo dos lundas, fazendo predominar os accentos nas ultimas syllabas.
new_statements.translation: The tonic accent falls almost always on the penultimate syllable, and for that very reason, with few exceptions, words are paroxytone, as can be seen from the examples already given. Few are oxytone, e.g. dizêu 'tooth', dičiadiá 'the day after tomorrow'. But paroxytones become oxytone when joined to other words, e.g. ŭape, ŭapé_kamo 'good, better'; ukŭete, ukŭeté_ŭoma 'has, is afraid', as was already noted on p. 6. Very few are proparoxytone, e.g. sâbaño 'six', tátuko 'father'. Observations. — I. The Bangala and the Chokwe already differ from the Lunda in making the accent fall predominantly on the final syllables.

The passage is there as quoted, section 'Vocabulos' of Parte I Phonologia: 'O accento tonico recae quasi sempre na penultima syllaba e por isso mesmo, com poucas excepções, os vocabulos são graves.. Poucos são os agudos, como: dizêu «dente», dičiad̃iá «depois de amanhã». Porém os graves tornam-se agudos unindo-se a outros. Ex.: ŭape, ŭapé_kamo.; ukŭete, ukŭeté_ŭoma.. Muito poucos são os esdruxulos ou proparoxytonos, como: sâb̃año «seis», tátuko «pai». Observações. — I. Os bângalas e os quiôcos já vão differindo dos lundas, fazendo predominar os accentos nas ultimas syllabas.' Only differences: the page prints Carvalho's nasal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Carvalho 1890 the 'tonic accent' is almost always on the penultimate syllable of the word (with final vowels still present in his 1890 forms); a few words are final-stressed, very few antepenultimate, and a penult-stressed word shifts its accent to its last syllable when it is joined (liaison) to a following word. Modern descriptions (Angenot & Vincke 1977, Ntotila & Vincke 1986, Nash 1994) treat Ruund as a two-tone language (marked L, default H, contrastive vowel length) and make no statement about word stress; Nash 1994 fn 44 notes only that abrupt-falling-pitch syllables have 'a certain accent-like prominence'.
new_statements.exceptions: Carvalho p. 11: a few oxytones (dizêu, dičiadiá), very few proparoxytones (sâbaño, tátuko); paroxytone > oxytone under liaison with a following word (ŭapé_kamo, ukŭeté_ŭoma); p. 7 Obs. II: when the last syllable contains a diphthong whose second element is ĭ or ŭ, that final syllable is the prominent one; p. 6 Obs. I: post-tonic vowels before a voiceless non-nasal consonant are whispered/nearly inaudible.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('vocabulo, simples ou composto, primitivo ou derivado'), with an explicit phrase-level shift under liaison. Caution: an 1890 pre-tonological description by a Portuguese army officer using Portuguese orthographic notions of 'accento tonico'; it never mentions tone, whereas all 20th-century descriptions are tone-only and silent on stress. Carvalho's forms keep final vowels that modern Ruund devoices/deletes (Nash 1994), so his 'penult' often corresponds to the final closed syllable of present-day citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source is Carvalho 1890, describing the 'lingua da Lunda' of the Muatiânvua's (Mwant Yav's) court at the Mussumba, recorded by the Portuguese expedition of 1884-88; Glottolog 5.1 assigns it to Ruund [rnd] = ruun1238 ('Lunda of the court of Mwant Yaav'). Two identity cautions from the book itself: (i) Carvalho's preface (p. 30) says he found that the dialects from Malanje to the Mussumba differ mainly in prefixes and endings and that he compiled the grammar using the rules he had observed for Ambundu (Kimbundu) at Malanje, so the description may be a composite shaped by Kimbundu-speaking interpreters; (ii) his forms retain final vowels (dizêu, tátuko, ŭape) that present-day Ruund reduces (Nash 1994: short final vowels devoiced then deleted except u; Ntotila & Vincke 1986: /a/ the only full vowel word-finally), though his note that post-tonic vowels are whispered (p. 6) matches Ruund's final-vowel devoicing. The modern tone descriptions cover the Musumban and Kalamban dialects (Nash 1994) and an informant from Ciying (Ntotila & Vincke 1986); Kanincin (Kabong 1985, Kasombo Tshibanda 2009) is treated by Glottolog as a Ruund variety with no separate glottocode.

tone_statements.citation: Kasombo Tshibanda, Michaël. 2022. Cuisiner ruwund à Kanincin : des mots pour le dire et des mets à savourer avec les linguistes. In Maud Devos & Birgit Ricquier (eds), Cooking with Linguists: Culinary Lexicon and Recipes in Selected Bantu Languages (Tervuren Series for African Language Documentation and Description), 21-100. Tervuren: Royal Museum for Central Africa. ISBN 978-9-4926-6974-2.
tone_statements.quote: Au niveau tonal, deux tons sont pertinents : le haut (á) et le bas (à). [...] Sinon, tout radical verbal est haut. Les fluctuations en termes d’abaissement de tonalités sont le résultat de la propagation d’un ton bas adjacent ou sous‑jacent qui se situe à la limite du morphème initial, [...] Cette propagation du ton bas demeure la principale caractéristique du ruwund comme du kanincin sur le plan tonal [...]. C’est dans ce contexte de propagation qu’apparaissent des tons modulés (descendant ou montant), le ton montant ne se limitant qu’aux verbes conjugués et à quelques formes pronominales. Sinon la séquence BH est en principe exclue.
tone_statements.translation: At the tonal level two tones are contrastive: high (á) and low (à). [...] Otherwise every verb radical is high. Fluctuations in the form of lowering of pitches result from the spreading of an adjacent or underlying low tone located at the boundary of the initial morpheme, [...] This low-tone spreading remains the main characteristic of Ruwund as of Kanincin at the tonal level [...]. It is in this spreading context that contour tones (falling or rising) appear, the rising tone being limited to conjugated verbs and a few pronominal forms. Otherwise the sequence LH is in principle excluded.
tone_statements.locator: p. 31, section '2. Lexique', introductory 'esquisse du kanincin', paragraph 'Au niveau tonal'
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (H, L) + derived falling (HL) and restricted rising (LH) contours

tone_statements.citation: Nash, Jay A. 1992-94 [1994]. Underlying low tones in Ruwund. Studies in African Linguistics 23(3): 223-278.
tone_statements.quote: In this paper the author examines data from Ruwund ... and proposes that, whereas most contemporary Bantu languages are believed to have tonal systems based on an underlying high/toneless contrast, Ruwund is based on a low/toneless contrast. Rules of tone spread and deletion apply to low tones rather than high tones, and the "default low insertion" rule of other languages is replaced in Ruwund by a rule adding default high tones. This finding ... contradicts Pulleyblank's [1986] proposal that "low" is always the default value in a two-tone language.
tone_statements.summary: Two tones: underlying L vs toneless, default H; surface falls/rises = H+L on bimoraic syllables; downstepped H from simplified rises; lexical tone in nouns, grammatical in verbs; low marks lost in txt.

sources.citation: Devos, Maud, Michael Kasombo Tshibanda & Johan van der Auwera. 2010. Jespersen cycles in Kanincin: double, triple and maybe even quadruple negation. Africana Linguistica 16: 155-181.
sources.quote: This paper studies the expression of standard negation in Kanincin, a variety of Ruund (L53), spoken in the Luilu territory of the East Kasai province of the DRC. [...] The Kanincin data are from Michael Kasombo Tshibanda, who is a native speaker of the language. [...] Other preverbal markers in Kanincin are known to induce such a lowering effect (Kasombo Tshibanda 2009 : 253)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress or accent placement; the only prosody discussed is tone (tonal lowering of subject-concord/tense material and of the stem under negation). Useful mainly as the authoritative citation of the Kasombo 2009 thesis and for placing Kanincin as a Ruund variety.

sources.citation: Nash, Jay A. 1992-94 [1994]. Underlying low tones in Ruwund. Studies in African Linguistics 23(3): 223-278.
sources.quote: Even in contemporary Ruwund, syllables bearing abrupt-falling pitch patterns have a certain accent-like prominence, and as observed earlier, the overall pitch range employed is not very wide. [p. 269 fn. 44] ... All nouns of pattern (e) appear to be borrowings from Swahili, a language with penultimate stress. [p. 272] ... The Ruwund vowels e and o are always long, as are vowels before nasal-initial consonant clusters in spellings. [p. 272 fn. 47]
sources.locator: p. 269 fn. 44; p. 272 (three-syllable nouns, pattern (e)); p. 272 fn. 47
sources.note: Treats Ruund as a two-tone (L-marked, default-H) language; no stress rule is given. Only accent-relevant remarks: falling-pitch syllables carry 'accent-like prominence' (a tonal, not positional, prominence), and one noun tone pattern is attributed to Swahili loans 'a language with penultimate stress' (implicitly contrasting Ruund). No statement of penultimate lengthening.

sources.citation: N'Landu, Ntotila & Jacques L. Vincke. 1986. Essai de tonologie générative du ruwund. Africana Linguistica 10: 315-335. DOI 10.3406/aflin.1986.932
sources.note: Generative tonology (informant Daniel Muland of Ciying; Kapanga/Musumb area). p. 317-318: three phonetic pitch levels, two simple tonemes H and L plus rising and falling, L is the marked toneme and H by far the most frequent; vowel quantity distinctive but neutralised in some contexts (R 18); /a/ the only full vowel word-finally; autonym [wùruwu:nd]. No word about accent/stress/intensity (a full-text search for stress/accent, intensité, proéminence, pénultième: none).

sources.citation: N., NLandu and Vincke, J. (1986). Essai de tonologie générative du ruwund. Africana Linguistica 121. pp. 315-336.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Says nothing about the penultimate 'accento tonico' the catalog records from Carvalho 1890; it neither confirms nor denies a stress system, but it shows that the modern tonological description of the same language (data from Daniel Muland of Ciying, Kapanga area around Musumb) needs no stress category, which is consistent with the catalog's caveat that Carvalho's 'accent' is a pre-tonal European-ear reading. It also warns (p. 317) that 'LUNDA' is ambiguous: Guthrie, White (1957) and Fisher (1963) use it for Ndembu (K.22), while in Zaire it is the heteronym of Ruwund, whose autonym is [wùruwu:…
